content.value: 22. SCHOLASTICISM: ITS NATURE AND PROBLEMS

The Meanings of“Scholasticism.” The diverse connotations of the word“scholasticism”make it desirable that we say something of its history and of the sense in which we shall use it. For our purpose we may neglect its earlier history and begin by noticing that it was applied in the time of Charlemagne to the teachings at the schools he established. A man designated as scholasticus might be supposed to be learned in the trivium (grammar, dialectic, rhetoric) and the Quadrivium (arithmetic, geometry, music, astronomy), or in theology. The application was gradually broadened in the course of time, until, finally, the title was given to any learned person, whether in the sciences or in philosophy, and whether a teacher or not. Throughout most of the medieval period it was a title of respect; but in the Renaissance period it became a term of contempt. The writers of the Renaissance considered Scholasticism barbaric on account of the presumed sophistry and pedantry of its representatives, and the alleged desiccation of its method.

Many modern historians of philosophy have tended to regard the Middle Ages as philosophically homogeneous, and have accordingly identified medieval philosophy and scholasticism. Some historians have based this identification solely on a chronological criterion; other historians have stressed the predominance of the didactic method, which they frequently assumed to be wholly deductive. Or again, the criterion has been the submission of reason to authority supposedly implicit in the theological orientation of most of the philosophy of the Middle Ages. But whatever standards were employed, the pejorative sense given the word scholasticism by the Renaissance has frequently been retained. In our own times, because of renewed interest in the philosophy of the Middle Ages, and, more particularly, because of the revival of the Thomastic philosophy, the original meaning of scholasticism has been reinstated, and many contemporary writers are proud to describe their philosophies as examples of a“new scholasticism.”

The historian De Wulf represents this new attitude and has given good historical reasons for rejecting a definition of scholasticism in terms of chronology, method, connection with the great medieval schools and universities, or deference to the authority of revelation. He admits that the dominant philosophy of the Middle Ages contains all these elements, but insists that it is also a doctrinal tradition. Such diverse figures as Anselm of Canterbury, Abelard, Alexander of Hales, St. Thomas Aquinas, and Duns Scotus, despite many disagreements, accept pluralism, spiritualism, and a belief in liberty, personal immortality, and the objectivity of human knowledge. To this core of scholasticism he opposes various anti-scholastic philosophies which advocate pantheistic monism, materialism, moral determinism, impersonal immortality, and subjectivism. To the anti-scholastic tendencies listed by De Wulf may be added two other important medieval interests outside the tradition culminating in St. Thomas Aquinas' philosophy: mysticism and natural science. We shall, then, define scholasticism as the dominant philosophy of the Middle Ages, associated with cloister or cathedral schools, and later with the universities, and possessing considerable continuity of method, doctrine, and problems.

As we have noted, scholasticism is best thought of as the line of development culminating in St. Thomas Aquinas, since his philosophy marks a peculiar poise in the history of thought—as it symbolizes a similar poise in the political sphere. Yet even this description of scholasticism is at times misleading, since the solutions to certain problems found within the scholastic tradition so defined are perfectly congruent with the solutions advanced by one or another of the so-called anti-scholastic tendencies. Thus, in the controversy over universals, a scholastic offering a solution in terms of extreme realism may find himself in complete agreement with a pantheist of the Neoplatonic tradition.

The Problems of Scholasticism. The essential continuity as well as the inner diversity of the scholastic tradition are best demonstrated by a survey of the development of certain central problems of scholasticism. For this purpose we have selected the following: (1) the relation between faith and reason, together with the not always identical question of the relation of revelation to reason; (2) the relation between the will and intellect; (3) the distinction between nature and grace—a problem which, for the present purposes at least, we may treat as ancillary to the first two; (4) the status of universals. To begin with any one of these problems is of course to find oneself very soon touching upon one of the others.

Relation of Faith and Reason. We have already considered the problem of faith and reason to the extent of showing how the acceptance of the Christian religion affected the standard of intelligibility held by the Christian philosophers, and caused them to reinterpret the categories received from antiquity. In this connection we were concerned with the inf l uence of Christian faith on the classical conception of reason, rather than with the explicit relation between faith and reason as sources of truth. Let us now turn to this question, and try to state the principal positions held on the subject by philosophers of the Middle Ages.

For St. Thomas Aquinas, faith is a gift from the Creator, completing a finite nature which, without it, would be truncated. Man's finite nature has a supernatural end: a beatitude consisting of the love and direct knowledge of God. To such a supernatural end the finite nature ought to conform; but, because the end is supernatural, man's nature can never attain it without assistance. Although the grace that confers faith comes in a sense from outside, yet, because it comes from a Creator who is responsible for the very existence of the creature in question, it works internally, so that faith appears as intrinsic to the nature it perfects. A nature so perfected by faith has therefore its intelligence perfected as well; and thus faith confers on the intellect, or reason, the ability to penetrate more deeply even in its own rational sphere. In this respect St. Thomas is at one with his master St. Augustine, even though they differ in defining the precise extent of what reason may achieve unaided.

The continuity of faith and reason, of grace and nature, is central to the thought of St. Thomas. In this context the important questions are: What can reason do in its own mode when it is the reason of someone who possesses faith? What ought reason to attempt to do? What are its concerns, and how should it limit itself? In his answers, St. Thomas insists throughout on the importance and penetration of the intellect in its own sphere, when that penetration is helped by faith. He finds that there are only a few things to which reason cannot attain—such as an adequate understanding of the Trinity—and there is nothing at all to the understanding of which it should not aspire, since, what is not attained in this life, is perhaps attainable in the next. The main ingredients of St. Thomas' position are: the continuity of faith and reason; the amplitude of reason and the independence of its concerns—an independence which makes possible a purely natural theology founded on reason alone; and the superiority of faith in this life, and of reason in the next.

St. Thomas' moderate position was preceded and followed historically by two forms of thought more extreme than his in their reliance—each in a different fashion—on faith. Before him, if we may oversimplify a highly diversified development, reason was ancillary to faith, having as its main purpose the rationalization of revealed truth. Most thinkers of this period felt that reason is quite competent to perform this function; indeed some of them, for example Berenger of Tours, Roscelin of Compiègne, and Abelard, carry this confidence in reason to a point where reason often seems to run counter to and to correct faith. In the period after St. Thomas there is less disposition to trust reason as a fit auxiliary for faith, and, as a result, revealed theology and faith came to be thought of as quite distinct from reason. This view so limits the activity of reason that, in natural theology at least, its province is meager or nonexistent. As a result of the discontinuity between the spheres of natural and revealed theology, reason, as exercised in the case of the latter, is nothing but faith in disguise. This radical separation of faith and reason, and the consequent skepticism regarding the powers of reason, seems to be progressive. According to Duns Scotus, reason, though diffident and restricted in scope, is still felt to be in eventual harmony with the insights of revealed theology; in the case of Occam and Nicholas of Autrecourt, reason is forced to abdicate totally from theology.

In both of these developments—that prior to St. Thomas, and that which follows him—faith plays a more important rôle than reason in that it alone insures our salvation. There is, however, a group of thinkers associated with Averroës which accepts as conclusive the arguments of reason, even if this means the modification or reinterpretation of received dogma. Siger of Brabant shows the influence of this tendency, and Occam's insistence that only faith is competent in matters of religion was in part a reaction to Siger. We shall later speak of the place in this movement of the doctrine of the twofold truth.

In the development prior to St. Thomas, we find in Berenger, Roscelin, and Abelard, a somewhat overconfident use of reason which tended to defeat its own initial purposes; philosophy is identified by them with dialectic. Berenger of Tours (1088) had an abounding trust in the dialectical method. To appeal to dialectic is to appeal to reason; and reason is that in us which makes us images of God; therefore, man's supreme good lies in following reason wherever it may lead him. This excessive rationalism led Berenger to a denial of two of the principal articles of faith. In a time that saw a restoration of the fervor of monastic life, there were many who attacked the overweening dialectical reason in the name of the truths of faith, and who urged that true knowledge is gained by adhering firmly to the truths of Scripture. Chief among these is Peter Damian (1007-1072), who will not hear of opposing to the divine power the puny necessities of human logic. The opposition between reason and faith becomes intensified in the twelfth century, when we find on the side of reason Roscelin of Compiègne ( ca . 1050- ca, 1120) and Abelard (1079-1142) and, on the side of faith, St. Bernard.

Abelard—always a contradictory figure—has many roots in the more moderate body of opinion that already existed at the time of the differences between Berenger and Damian. Lanfrance of Bec and Canterbury (1105-1089), a contemporary of Berenger, has already maintained that it was quite proper to confirm faith by reason, indeed, that dialectic can be used to sustain and confirm revelation, since there is no real contradiction between faith and reason when reason is properly employed. St. Anselm (1033-1109) summarizes in this spirit the wisdom of his master St. Augustine in the formula credo ut intelligam (“I believe in order that I may understand”), by which he means that of the two powers by which we attain knowledge, or apprehension, faith is the controlling one. Truth is so vast that the knowledge contained in the Scriptures cannot claim to exhaust that which is attainable by us; therefore, to comprehend by reason the faith contained in Scripture is to approach closer to the vision of God. We are obligated not only to believe the mysteries of faith, but to force reason to comprehend them. There is scarcely an important truth of faith—including the doctrine of the Incarnation—of which Anselm does not attempt to give a logical demonstration; and in so doing he is much more confident than St. Thomas. The latter would, however, accord to the unaided reason more scope than does Anselm; for St. Thomas holds that there is a group of truths, such as the mysteries of the Trinity, the Incarnation, and the Redemption, quite incapable of justification by reason. Others, belonging in some measure to the Augustinian tradition represented by Anselm, engaged in enterprises similar to his, though without restricting their activities to religious matters. Thus Roger Bacon (1214-1292) and Raymond Lull (d. 1315) attempted complete explanations of the most abstruse doctrinal matters in terms, respectively, of geometrical figures, and a symbolic calculus. In yet another Augustinian, St. Bonaventure, a theology dominated by faith seems almost to supplant philosophy; for although St. Bonaventure preserved knowledge as an adjunct to faith, he allowed grace to penetrate even the lowliest operations of the mind.

Before St. Thomas, then, the dominant tone is one of confidence in reason as an adjunct to faith, even though reason may at times seem overweening, and at other times be unrecognizable. If we now turn to the distrust of reason that sets in after the thirteenth century, we encounter the doctrine of twofold truth, which may be interpreted as undermining either reason or faith, depending upon whether emphasis is placed on the religious truths of faith or the secular truths of reason.

The source of the theory of the twofold truth of the later Middle Ages may be traced principally to Siger of Brabant ( ca . 1235- ca . 1281), the famous opponent of St. Thomas, who held that on certain questions two answers could be given, one by revelation, and one by reason, and that these answers might be contradictory. Siger, whether out of prudence, or out of a deference to religion understandable in even the most radical thinkers of those times, somewhat mitigates the opposition by reserving the name“truth”for the content of revelation, so that the theory is, strictly speaking, not one of a twofold truth, but a conflict between revelation understood as truth and philosophy understood as natural knowledge. In its extreme form, the theory of the twofold truth holds that a doctrine may be true from the point of view of faith, even when our reason tells us that it is false.

Unlike Siger, Duns Scotus ( ca . 1270-1308) believes in the harmony of faith and reason: he considers theology founded on faith a practical science, more concerned with our salvation than our enlightenment, within which rational and necessary demonstrations are indeed possible, but only, in Anselmian fashion, when the articles demonstrated are first believed. To this practical“science”is opposed the natural reason of philosophy, which is incapable of proving many of the truths which St. Thomas held to be accessible to it. Although he does not yet go so far as to deny that the existence of God is susceptible to proof, this drastic step is taken by William of Occam in the fourteenth century. Occam's adoption of this extreme position results from his critical analysis of the human reason, together with a genuine desire to preserve the truths of the faith against such destructive criticism. According to Occam's nominalistic theory, our knowledge of the world of particulars yields only probability, even in such matters as the proof of the existence of God as a prime mover. But such knowledge is clearly inadequate for the purposes of natural theology. Occam is led by these considerations to exclude theology entirely from the domain of natural or rational knowledge, and thus to adopt the theory of the twofold truth.

The Occamist Nicholas of Autrecourt, who attempts to save Occam's position from extreme skepticism, restricts himself to so few certainties as to give philosophy small comfort; and in any case he has no wish to extend such comfort, since he is primarily concerned with saving the religious and moral life from the uncertainties of the reasoning process. The closing period of the Middle Ages is characterized by a combination of empiricism, nominalism, skepticism, and religious faith in which the spirit of modern science can already be discerned, as also can the Reformation's attitude toward faith.

Relation of Will to Intellect. We find echoes of the faith vs. reason controversy when we turn to the important question as to whether the higher of the two principal faculties of the soul is the will or the intellect. For the Middle Ages thought of faith as primarily engaging the will, whereas reasoning, by definition, engaged the intellect. In one of its forms the question is whether action of the will is able to generate intellectual ideas, or whether the intellect on its own initiative presents the will with alternatives in the form of ideas. The question of the nature of that free will, which it is a major concern of all Christian philosophers to defend, is of course here at issue. Any discussion of the will in scholastic philosophy is complicated by the connection between the will and a divinely ordained grace which supposedly moves the will. The basic question at issue is whether the will, as the higher faculty, is absolutely self-determining; or whether the will is itself determined by knowledge of the good. The lines of controversy are fairly cleanly drawn between Augustinians (including Scotus and Occam) as advocates of the will, and Aristotelians, as advocates of the intellect. This division, in the late Middle Ages, often coincides with the division between Franciscans and Dominicans. Although it is convenient and in many respects correct to think of St. Thomas as an Aristotelian, he can be so regarded here only with many qualifications. It is also important that we speak here once more of Augustinians, rather than of St. Augustine, for many systems have been elaborated from their non-systematic founder. It would seem at first that St. Augustine should not appear in this controversy, since he likens the unity of existence, will, and intellect in the human person to the unity of being, movement, and order in the Trinity. But despite this insistence on the unity of the personality, he emphasizes dynamism so strongly as to seem to make the will the leading faculty, and he was so interpreted by many disciples.

Once again, we shall begin by outlining the position of St. Thomas Aquinas; and we shall find in it a moderation which makes it impossible to class it with the purely intellectualist positions. It is frequently said that for St. Thomas the intellect determines the will, and Windelband goes so far as to call his position an“intellectualistic determinism.”“The intellect,”he says in his account of St. Thomas, “not only apprehends in general the idea of the good, but also, in each individual case, discerns what is good, and thereby determines the will.” ［8］ We shall have more to say later regarding the views of St. Thomas on the relation between will and intellect in individual moral or cognitive acts; but we should note at once that his position on faith and love gives him much more in common with Augustine than is perhaps generally recognized. St. Thomas felt that it is better to love an object of the greatest magnitude than to know it imperfectly. Because of our limitations in this life he sees love of God as our highest function, and takes faith, understood as a gift of grace, to be the mode of apprehension corresponding to this love. In faith and in the love of God, the will is the one of our faculties which is most involved, and the operative power in the transaction, according to the doctrine of grace, is the object—God—rather than the subject —man. In this context St. Thomas' intellectualism appears rather in his doctrine of the after-life where, because possession is considered to be better than desire, and because understanding is identified with possession, beatitude is said to consist of knowledge of the essence of God. The will's love of God is a consequence of this activity of the intellect and it is only at this point that the position of St. Thomas can be seen to be clearly opposed to that of Duns Scotus, who teaches that beatitude consists of an activity of the will in which the creature is directed wholly to God by love.

By an extension of the principle just enunciated, St. Thomas holds that in this life, and in the case of finite objects, possession by the intellect is a higher activity than that of the will; hence, that it is better to know than to believe. We are therefore to seek to know and to demonstrate all that we can know; in the case of the Deity, this will be the subject matter of natural theology. But at the same time the will should be ever alert, and we should be prepared to believe and love when demonstration is impotent or would be an impertinence.

When we turn to the relation between the faculties of will and intellect in a given cognitive or moral act, we find an even clearer opposition between Duns Scotus and St. Thomas Aquinas, but one which it is difficult to describe without exaggeration. For the former, the intellect, whether of God or man, is associated with the notion of the determinate and the natural. In finite creatures the natural movement of the intellect by its object must be performed before the will can add its voluntary motion; and here“voluntary”and“natural”are thought of as in opposition. This distinction in man is parallel to the distinction in God between his knowledge of his own determinate nature, and the absolutely voluntary and free decision by which he makes actual the things which, though he discerns them in his essence, move him only contingently. Everything, then, if it is free, whether in God or man, belongs to will, which is a principle of indetermination; and everything that is necessary or determinate is natural; and this includes the intellect. While more rationalistic theories claim that the alternatives proposed by the intellect make a freedom of choice possible, the voluntaristic theory of Scotus ascribes liberty to a spontaneous act of will, which, after deliberation, decides between alternatives. On this issue as on others, tendencies noticeable in Scotus are intensified in Occam; the latter holds that the very goodness of a good thing is derived from the decree of God.

The position of St. Thomas, while in general it emphasizes the intellect, has certain features in common with the doctrine of Duns Scotus. Taking the will as the source of all movement in an entity, St. Thomas insists upon its absolute spontaneity or indetermination—freedom in its radical sense. The being may give or withhold its action—a man freely wills to think or not to think a certain good. We may argue that the will moves even the intellect to apprehend its object. But the will is only incompletely defined by its spontaneity and indetermination, and must also include a valuational element, in that the will seeks goods, and indeed necessarily wills at least one good—beatitude. Furthermore, the will is in close association with the intellect in this valuational activity, for not only does it move the intellect to apprehend its objects, but it is among the objects apprehended by the intellect. It is obvious, whatever the difficulties of formulation, that St. Thomas intends a complex definition of free will in which indetermination, or indifference, ［9］ is supplemented by other characteristics. But it is also obvious that this very supplementation produces difficulties of formulation which, in the case of the relation between will and intellect, may be summarized in the paradox that while the will is that in us which moves us to action, including the action which is knowledge, it can nevertheless only will a good which has been presented to it by the intellect.“The reason reasons about willing, and the will wills to reason.” ［10］

Let us now turn to another characteristic of the will—its power to attain the objects proper to man's nature and the supernatural object for which man is ultimately intended. Here we find other difficulties, which are perhaps most apparent when we consider the problem of faith; for faith is not only a prerequisite to salvation, but the proper understanding of the meaning of faith requires, according to St. Thomas, an understanding of grace and free will and of the relation between them. St. Thomas tells us that“by assenting to what belongs to faith, man is raised above his nature.”Faith, therefore, must needs come to him from some supernatural principle moving him inwardly. . . faith, as regards the assent which is its chief act, is God moving man inwardly by grace To believe does indeed depend on the will of the believer; but man's will needs to be prepared by God with grace, in order that he may be raised to things which are above his nature. . . . ［11］

The complete description of this will that is said to be free must, then, include some account of its power to attain its object; and once more the intention is to preserve the freedom even when the power seems to come from elsewhere:

. . . God moves everything in its own manner. . . . But it is proper to man's nature to have free choice. Hence in him who has the use of free choice God's motion to justice does not take place without a movement of the free choice; but He so infuses the gift of justifying grace that at the same time He moves free choice to accept the gift of grace in such as are capable of being moved thus. ［12］ God helps us, as St. Augustine said, even to help ourselves.

The difficulties of formulation here, and in the case of the relation between will and intellect—where the inherited Aristotelian terminology presents its own problems—should not blind us to the fact that, as in the case of St. Augustine, an attempt is being made to maintain a position which is neither voluntarism nor a strict intellectual determinism. The problem of freedom is one in which philosophers often find formulation at odds with intent. It is possible that many of these difficulties disappear when rightly regarded: the act of creation need not be thought of as analogous to manufacture, but may be regarded as the sustaining of a creation from within or, as the phrase goes, it is creation with time, rather than in time. Thus the freedom of the creature is the act of a coadjutor in creation, and grace is a bridge between an infinite creator and a finite creation—a bridge clearly necessary to save the meaning of the“ought”with which the creature is confronted. In any case, the tendency of the late Middle Ages was toward a separation between will and intellect, faith and reason, grace and nature, incompatible with the earlier doctrine of freedom which sought—with however little success—a theory in which indetermination, value, and power mingled with and qualified the relations existing between will and intellect, and between free will and grace.

The Problem of Universals. We shall treat the problem of universals somewhat more briefly, since it is discussed at some length in the sections that follow. The controversy has its foundation in the following passage from Boethius' Latin version of Porphyry's Introduction to the Categories of Aristotle:“Next as to genera and species, do they actually exist, or are they merely in thought; are they corporeal or incorporeal existences; are they separate from sensible things or only in and of them? I refuse to answer; it is a very lofty business, unsuited to an elementary work.”Porphyry's warning to beginners went unheeded, and on this suggestive speculation-for so it must have seemed to the earliest medieval writers, since they did not know that Porphyry had an answer he deemed satisfactory—the early Middle Ages founded its principal purely philosophical disputations.

As we have seen, these disputes could at first be sustained only on certain parts of the Aristotelian logic, as well as on Neoplatonic and Augustinian material; but this did not prevent the formulation of extremely complex answers even before the appearance of Aristotelian metaphysics widened their range. The answers given throughout the Middle Ages are of three types: (1) Those philosophers who hold that genera and species have a real existence, independent both of the mind that entertains them and the world of individuals that may be presumed to exemplify them, are spoken of as realists . Their doctrine may be combined with a derogation of the world of sense, and a theory of knowledge that we may loosely designate as Platonic; or, in accord with the Christian desire to save a world of individual concrete substances, it may take only the shape of insisting that the individual thing be conceived primarily in terms of its formal or structural elements. (2) At the other pole is the formula that only the individual is real, in so strict a way as to maintain that so-called genera and species“are simply names by means of which we designate resembling individuals. In its extreme and more naïve form this nominalism insists on the general term as a mere name, a mere word, or even as a mere sound. In its more subtle form, nominalism, while retaining the view that these general terms are in any case mental, gives attention to the meanings involved; the doctrine is then known as sermonism (Abelard) or terminism (Occam). This version of the doctrine is sometimes referred to by modern writers as conceptualism . (3) Mediating between nominalism and realism is a third position, which depends for its formulation on the Aristotelian theory of knowledge, and therefore upon the Aristotelian analysis of the individual substance into components of form and matter. This position, which is designated by its advocates as moderate realism, shares with nominalism only the disposition to regard the individual as ultimate; but it agrees with realism in accepting what is common to Plato and Aristotle. This is not the place to discuss the question whether Aristotle is not, in the long run, quite close to Plato in so far as he insists that the immanent form confers actuality upon the ultimate individual substance. We may indeed note that this form is identifiable with the essence of the individual; that the essence is that in the individual which renders it definable; and that, therefore, the form is identifiable with that which the individual has in common with other members of the same species. But we must then add that this form can nevertheless have a non-mental existence only as belonging to an individual concrete substance, composed of form and matter—a concrete substance in which the matter is the individuating factor. For the moderate realism of St. Thomas, which presupposes Aristotle's theory of knowledge, the composite of form and matter is one of essence and existence; but in order for the mind to entertain the essence, and thereby give it the universality it lacks as an element in the concrete individual, there must be present to the knower an existing concrete individual, from which abstraction can be made. The universal, then, has a threefold existence: it exists in the individual, but not precisely as universal; after abstraction it has an existence grounded on that in the individual, but with an added note of universality; and finally, by way of the influence of St. Augustine's exemplarism, St. Thomas thinks of genera and species as existing before individuals, in the mind of God. But even here the intent of the Aristotelian emphasis on the individual has been retained by the insistence that these exemplars are merely the ways in which aspects of God's essence may be imitated in an imperfect way by individual things: it is, so to speak, because God is a being, that he may discern ways in which his being may be participated in.

Realism in an extreme form is the dominant solution during the very earliest times of our period. We may here first note the Neoplatonic variety of John Scotus Erigena, in which highest generality is associated with highest reality. In the course of the subsequent development of scholastic philosophy, however, nominalism very quickly comes to the fore. It is associated at first with Aristotle's logic which, being more purely formal than his metaphysics, might easily give the impression that it relates primarily to words rather than to things. In its earlier forms, there is no suspicion that a nominalistic position tends to undermine the adequacy of our knowledge; it is only in their rôles of overconfident dialecticians that Roscelin and his sometime pupil Abelard came into conflict with the theologians. It is chiefly in the theological debate with Anselm who, being an Augustinian, is also a realist, that nominalism loses countenance in the early Middle Ages. Roscelin did not hesitate to insist that his nominalism renders suspect our formulation of the Trinity, if not the intent of our devotions, and the theologian St. Anselm is equally insistent that the articles of our faith—felt to be demonstrable—require realism as a basis for this demonstrability. Many of Anselm's arguments—in particular the famous ontological argument-depend upon the assumption that degree of understood perfection is equivalent to degree of being; or, expressed differently, that it is possible to go from essence to existence.

The reader will note parallels with what we have already said about St. Anselm's views on the relation between faith and reason. In much of the scholasticism of the twelfth and thirteenth centuries, realism, either in this extreme Augustinian-Platonic form, or in the more moderate Aristotelian position exemplified by St. Thomas, is dominant; and the compromise of Abelard, who differed from his teacher Roscelin as well as from another teacher, the realist William of Champeaux, is on the whole unsuccessful. Nominalism revives again in the later Middle Ages; at this time it is associated with the waning confidence in the harmony of faith and reason which we have already noted. If we deal with terms or concepts only, and if the world of the individual is ultimate, and alone accessible to direct observation, then the rationalistic science used by St. Thomas to support faith must gradually be superseded by the empirical science that comes to maturity in the seventeenth century.
